HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) must receive your tax return and any money you owe by the deadline.

If you do not know your profit for the whole tax year, you still need to send a tax return. Check how to send a return if you do not know your profit for the whole year.

The last tax year started on 6 April 2025 and ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier tax returns has passed. You may have to pay a penalty. Send your tax return or payment as soon as possible to avoid further penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to complete a return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to complete a tax return for the previous year. You must tell them if you have either:

- not sent a tax return before
- registered before but did not need to send a tax return for the tax year 2024 to 2025

You can tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email with a different deadline to send your tax return by. This deadline will be 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty.

## Sending a paper tax return

HMRC must get your paper tax return by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026.  
If you miss this, you will get a late filing penalty.

You can send it any time from 6 April 2026.  
HMRC must still get it before the deadline.

### Submitting an online tax return

You must submit your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027.
If you do not, you will get a late filing penalty.

If you want to pay your Self Assessment bill through your tax code, you must submit it by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026.
If you miss this deadline, you will have to pay another way.

You can submit your return any time on or after 6 April 2026.
You must submit it by the deadline.

## Paying the tax you owe

You must pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027.  
If you do not pay by this time, you will get a penalty.  
There is a second payment deadline of 31 July.  
You only make payments on this date if you make payments towards your bill.  
These payments are called 'payments on account'.  
You can estimate your Self Assessment tax bill before you send your tax return.  
Estimating the bill can give you an idea of what your bill is likely to be.  
Estimating the bill can also allow you to budget and pay on time.  
Find help on understanding the tax you owe.

## Trustees of a registered pension scheme or non-resident companies

HMRC must get a paper tax return. The deadline is 31 January 2027. You cannot send the return online. You can send it any time on or after 6 April 2026. HMRC must get it by the deadline.

### Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

If your partnership’s accounting date is between 1 February and 5 April and one of your partners is a limited company, the deadline is:

- 12 months from the accounting date for online returns
- 9 months from the accounting date for paper returns

You will get a penalty if you need to file a tax return and you:

- send your return late

- pay your tax bill late

You can estimate your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

## If you register for Self Assessment late

If you register after 5 October, you may get a penalty.

Do not pay all your tax by 31 January.

This penalty is based on the amount left to pay.

HMRC will send the penalty within 12 months.

This starts after HMRC gets your Self Assessment tax return.

You can find more information on ‘failure to notify’ penalties.

## If you send your tax return late

You will get late filing penalties.

- You get an initial £100 penalty.
- After 3 months, you get daily penalties of £10 per day.
- These daily penalties can go up to a maximum of £900.
- After 6 months, you pay another penalty.
- This 6 months penalty is 5% of the tax due or £300.
- You pay whichever amount is greater.
- After 12 months, you pay another charge.
- This charge is 5% or £300.
- You pay whichever amount is greater.

Send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as possible to avoid this.

All partners get charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

## If you pay your tax late

You get a penalty of 5% of the tax unpaid.
You get this penalty after 30 days.
You get this penalty after 6 months.
You get this penalty after 12 months.
You also pay interest on the amount you owe.
Pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as possible to avoid this.
Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

### Your State Pension

Your State Pension amount depends on your National Insurance record.

Check your State Pension forecast. This tells you how much you could get at State Pension age. It also shows your National Insurance record.

The full rate of new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your amount could be different depending on:

- if you were contracted out before 2016
- the number of National Insurance qualifying years you have
- if you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Find out what tax you might pay on your retirement income. This includes if you retire abroad.

## If you’re getting less than £241.30 a week

You might need more National Insurance qualifying years to increase your State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been contracted out. You or your employer paid more into your workplace or private pension while you were contracted out. You or your employer paid less into your State Pension while you were contracted out. If you were contracted out, you will usually need more than 35 qualifying years. You will need more than 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

If your National Insurance record started after April 2016, you will need 35 qualifying years. You will need 35 qualifying years to get the full rate of new State Pension.

### If you're getting more than £241.30 a week

If you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016, you might get a 'protected payment'. You will get this if you would have got more State Pension under the old rules. This 'protected payment' is added on top of the full rate of new State Pension.

### Annual increases

Your new State Pension goes up every year.

The amount is the biggest of these three numbers:

- earnings, which is the average rise in wages in Great Britain
- prices, which is the rise in UK prices measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)
- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, your pension rises every year with the CPI.

There are 2 Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |
| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

You must contact the Child Benefit Office if you are paid too much or too little.

Any Child Benefit payments you get will count towards the benefit cap. If you are affected by the cap, you will still get the full amount for your Child Benefit payments. Your other benefits may be reduced.

## If families split up

If a family splits up, you get £27.05 a week for the eldest child.

If you have 2 children, the math changes.
One child lives with you.
The other child lives with someone else.
This could be your ex-partner.
You get £27.05 a week for your child.
They get £27.05 a week for their child.
Only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child.
If you both claim, only one of you gets the money.
You get £17.90 for each other child.

### If families join together

If you move in with a partner, you get £27.05 for the eldest child.  
Your partner may also claim for their children.  
You cannot both claim the higher rate.  
The higher rate is £27.05 per eldest child.  
If you both claim it, you may have to pay back money.  
You must tell us about this change.

## If you or your partner earn over the threshold

If you or your partner has an adjusted net income over the threshold, you may have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge.

Your adjusted net income is your total taxable income before any personal allowances. You must subtract things like Gift Aid from this total. Your total taxable income includes interest from savings. It also includes dividends.

If you have to pay the charge, you can still get other advantages. These include National Insurance credits. The charge will not be more than the amount you get from Child Benefit payments.

Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to check if your adjusted net income is over the threshold. If it is, the calculator will tell you how much charge you must pay.

If both you and your partner have an individual income over the threshold, the person with the higher adjusted net income pays the charge.

If either you or your partner has an individual income of £20,000 or more above the threshold, you get charged the full amount of your Child Benefit payments. This amount is £10,000 or more before April 2024. You will end up with no extra money from Child Benefit.

You can make a claim and opt out of getting payments if you do not want to pay the charge. You can still get the other advantages provided by Child Benefit. These include National Insurance credits.

## If you’re under 16

You can claim for your own child.
Or someone responsible for you can claim for them on your behalf.
You’ll usually get more if you claim yourself.

Universal Credit is paid once every month.
The amount you receive depends on your standard allowance.
It depends on any extra amounts that apply to you.
It depends on any money taken off your payment.
It depends on how much you earn if you are working.
You can see how much you could get by using a benefits calculator.
If you get Universal Credit, you will earn Class 3 National Insurance credits.
These credits count towards your State Pension.

## Standard allowance

You get one standard allowance for your household.

| How much you’ll get | Monthly standard allowance |
| | |
| If you’re single and under 25 | £338.58 |
| If you’re single and 25 or over | £424.90 |
| If you live with your partner and you’re both under 25 | £528.34 (for you both) |
| If you live with your partner and either of you are 25 or over | £666.97 (for you both) |

## Extra amounts

You may get more money than your standard allowance if you are eligible.

You must tell the government when you become eligible for extra money.

Extra amounts are not added automatically.

For example, if you become a carer, you need to tell the DWP.

The carer's element of Universal Credit is not applied automatically if you start getting Carer's Allowance.

### If you have children

You will get £303.94 each month for every child who lives with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you get an extra £47.94 each month for that child.

You get money for each child until 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training – for example, they are studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

### If your child has a disability

You might get extra money each month if any of your children are disabled.

You will get one of these amounts:

- £164.79 - the lower amount

- £514.71 - the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you are working.

If you live with your partner, both of you must be working.

One of you does not need to work if they cannot work due to a disability or health condition.

The childcare must be from a registered provider.

You can get help paying for childcare including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You need to pay your childcare costs up front and claim the money back as part of your payment.

You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front.

Talk to your work coach after you have made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You might get extra money each month if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you'll get | Extra monthly amount |

| If you have a severe health condition or disability that's unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |

| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you will only get one extra monthly amount.

You will get the higher amount if one of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you are moving to Universal Credit, you might also be entitled to a 'transitional protection' payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount known as a 'carer's element'.

This is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of the following benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You need to provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You will get an extra monthly amount of £209.34.

If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you will only get one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer's Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work related activity (LCWRA), you cannot also get the carer's element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it will stop when you claim the carer's element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs.

The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you are a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken off your payment

Your payment might get smaller.

This can happen if any of these are true:

- You are paying back an advance on a Universal Credit payment
- You would get above the amount limited by the benefit cap
- You have been overpaid benefits in the past
- You owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance
- You pay your gas or electricity bill directly from your Universal Credit payment
- You have a paid job
- You have other income. This can be money from pensions or certain other benefits
- You have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have over £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment will be reduced by £4.35.

This is for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000.

Another £4.35 is taken off for any remaining amount that is not a complete £250.

Find out more about money taken off your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that affect how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit at the same time as other benefits.

Your Universal Credit payment will be reduced.

The reduction will be equal to the other benefit’s payment.

This applies when you get Universal Credit and any of the following benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions
- Carer's Allowance
- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)
- Incapacity Benefit
- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (excluding any increases where constant attendance is needed and for exceptionally severe disablement)
- Maternity Allowance
- Severe Disablement Allowance
- State Pension
- Widowed Mother's Allowance
- Widowed Parent's Allowance
- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)
- New Style Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA)

### Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA

You might be able to get Universal Credit at the same time as New Style ESA or JSA.
If you do, your Universal Credit payment is reduced by the amount you get for New Style ESA or JSA.
New Style ESA and JSA are paid more regularly than Universal Credit.
You will also get different National Insurance credits.
These credits count towards your State Pension.
They can help you qualify for other benefits.
You might continue to get New Style ESA or JSA if your circumstances change.
Your Universal Credit payment might be reduced or stop.
For example, this could happen if:
- your partner’s income increases
- you have more than £16,000 in savings
Check if you're eligible for:
- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance
- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

## Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you apply for Universal Credit, you keep getting your current benefit for 2 more weeks.
You must still be eligible for your current benefit.

This only applies if you are getting income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Housing Benefit.

You will not need to pay back the extra payments.
They will not affect the Universal Credit you might get.

If you get a Migration Notice letter telling you to claim Universal Credit, you might also get a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

## If your Universal Credit claim is reviewed

Your claim might be reviewed. This makes sure you get the right payment. It also makes sure you get the right support. Find out more about Universal Credit reviews.

You may get Carer’s Allowance.  
This depends on you.  
This depends on the person you care for.  
This depends on the care you give.  
All of them must meet certain rules.

## The person you care for

The person you care for must already get one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component

- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate

- Attendance Allowance

- Pension Age Disability Payment

- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate

- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer’s Allowance if you share the care of someone.

The other carer must not already claim one of these for that person:

- Carer’s Allowance for that person

- Carer Support Payment for that person

- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit for that person

You can speak to the other carer about changing their benefits.

If you want to get Carer’s Allowance, ask them to make a change.

If the other carer does not want to do that, you can still apply for Carer’s Allowance.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should receive the benefit.

### The type of care you provide

You must care for someone for 35 hours a week. You can help with washing and cooking. You can take the person to a doctor’s appointment. You can help with household tasks. This includes managing bills and shopping.

## Your eligibility

All of these rules must be true for you:

- You are 16 or over.

- You spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone.

- You have been in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years. This rule does not apply if you are a refugee or have humanitarian protection status.

- You normally live in England or Wales. Or you live abroad as a member of the armed forces. You might still be eligible if you are moving to or already living in an EEA country or Switzerland.

- You are not in full-time education.

- You are not studying for 21 hours a week or more.

- You are not subject to immigration control.

- Your earnings are £204 or less a week after tax, National Insurance and expenses.

If you live in Scotland, you need to apply for Carer Support Payment instead of Carer’s Allowance.

If you are from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein, you and your family usually need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme to get Carer’s Allowance. The deadline to apply to the scheme was 30 June 2021 for most people. But you might still be able to apply. Check if you can still apply to the EU Settlement Scheme.

### Calculating your earnings

Your earnings are any income from employment and self-employment after tax, National Insurance and expenses.

Expenses can include:

- 50% of your pension contributions

- equipment you need to do your job, for example specialist clothing

- travel costs between different workplaces that are not paid for by your employer, for example fuel or train fares

- business costs if you're self-employed, for example a computer you only use for work

If you pay a carer to look after the disabled person or your children while you work, you can treat care costs that are less than or equal to 50% of your earnings as an expense. The carer must not be your spouse, partner, parent, child or sibling.

Example

You earn £100 a week (after tax, National Insurance and other expenses) and spend £60 a week on care while you work. You can treat £50 of this as an expense.

Payments that do not count as earnings include:

- money received from an occupational or private pension

- contributions towards your living or accommodation costs from someone you live with (they cannot be a tenant or boarder)

- the first £20 a week and 50% of the rest of any income you make from someone boarding in your home

- a loan or advance payment from your employer

### If you get State Pension

You cannot get the full Carer’s Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer’s Allowance payment.

If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you will get a Carer’s Allowance payment. This payment makes up the difference.

## If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, you will not get a Carer's Allowance payment. Your Pension Credit payments will increase instead.

### Pension Credit tops up:

- It adds money to your weekly income if you are single.
- This raises your weekly income to £238.
- It adds money to your weekly income if you have a partner.
- This raises your joint weekly income to £363.25.

You may get extra amounts if you have other responsibilities and costs.

The top up and extra amounts are known as ‘Guarantee Credit’.

## If you have a severe disability

You could get an extra £86.05 a week.

You could get this extra money if you get any of these benefits:

- Attendance Allowance
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)
- the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance

## If you care for another adult

You could get an extra £48.15 a week.

- You can get this if you get Carer’s Allowance.
- You can get this if you get Carer Support Payment.
- You can get this if you have claimed Carer’s Allowance. You are not being paid because you already get another benefit. This other benefit pays a higher amount.

You and your partner can both get this extra amount. You do not have to check who claimed. You both must have claimed or be getting Carer’s Allowance.

## If you're responsible for children or young people

You may get extra money for each child or young person living with you.

You will get £69.98 a week for each one.

This amount is £81.07 a week for your first child if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You will get this extra money until 31 August after one of these events:

- Their 16th birthday

- Their 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training

They could be studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers, SVQs or NVQs up to level 3.

They must study for more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

If the child or young person is disabled, you may get extra money.

You may get an extra £37.93 a week if they get one of these:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component

- Child Disability Payment - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component

- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component

- Adult Disability Payment - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component

You may get an extra £118.46 a week if they get one of these:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - highest rate of the care component

- Child Disability Payment - highest rate of the care component

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - highest rate of the care component

- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - enhanced rate of the daily living component

- Adult Disability Payment - enhanced rate of the daily living component

You might also qualify if they are blind or severely sight impaired.

### If you have housing costs

You could get extra money to pay for your housing costs.

This money can cover:
- ground rent if your property is leasehold
- some service charges
- charges for tents and site rents

The extra amount depends on your housing costs.

If you get Pension Credit, you could also get:
- Council Tax Reduction
- Housing Benefit if you rent the property you live in
- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own the property you live in

## If you have savings or a second pension

You could get the 'Savings Credit' part of Pension Credit if two things are true.

*   you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016
*   you saved some money for retirement, for example a personal or workplace pension

You could get up to £17.96 Savings Credit a week if you are single. If you have a partner, you could get up to £20.10 a week.

You could still get some Savings Credit even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

## Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit, you get cold weather payments automatically.

You can also:

- apply for a free TV licence if you are 75 or older
- get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include prescriptions.
NHS costs can include dental treatment.
NHS costs can include glasses.
NHS costs can include transport costs for hospital appointments.

## Get help with extra amounts

Contact the Pension Service helpline if you’re not sure if you get extra amounts.

### Pension Service helpline

**Telephone:** 0800 99 1234

**Relay UK (if you cannot hear or speak on the phone):** 18001 then 0800 99 1234

**British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service** if you’re on a computer - find out how to use the service on mobile or tablet

**Open:** Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm (except public holidays)

Find out about call charges

### Statutory Maternity Pay

Statutory Maternity Pay lasts for 39 weeks. You receive money in two parts.

- You get 90% of your average weekly earnings before tax for the first 6 weeks.
- You get £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings for the next 33 weeks. You take the lower amount.

Statutory Maternity Pay comes like your normal wages. It can be monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance are taken out.

Use the maternity planner to work out your pay.

If you take Shared Parental Leave, you get Statutory Shared Parental Pay. This is called ShPP. ShPP is £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings. You take the lower amount.

## Start date

SMP usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

It starts automatically if you are off work for a pregnancy-related illness.

This must happen in the 4 weeks before your baby is due.

The week is counted from Sunday to Saturday.

### Problems and disputes

Ask your employer to explain your SMP if you think it is not right. If you disagree about the amount, contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team. If your employer cannot pay, contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team.

If you qualify, you can get £123.25 a week Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) or 80% of your normal weekly earnings.
Choose the lower amount of those two figures.
It is paid for up to 28 weeks.
You get SSP for all the full days you are off sick.
Only count days you normally would have worked.
Your employer will use your average weekly earnings over an 8-week period.
They will use this to work out how much you get.
You still qualify if you started your job recently.
You still qualify if you have not yet received 8 weeks' pay.
Ask your employer to find out more.

## How you're paid

Your employer pays SSP like your normal wages.

They might pay you weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, each employer may pay you SSP.

Tax and National Insurance are deducted.

If you think your SSP amount is wrong, talk to your employer.

If you are still not happy, contact the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

The minimum wage depends on your age. It also depends on whether you are an apprentice.

### This page is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

You must be at least school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage.

You must be aged 21 to get the National Living Wage.

The National Living Wage is the minimum wage for workers aged 20 and under.

## Current rates

The rates change on 1 April every year.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |

| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |

| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

Apprentices get the apprentice rate if they are under 19.

Apprentices get the apprentice rate if they are 19 or over and in their first year.

Example

An apprentice aged 21 in their first year gets £8.

Apprentices get the minimum wage for their age if they are 19 or over.

Apprentices get the minimum wage for their age if they have finished their first year.

Example

An apprentice aged 21 who has finished their first year gets £12.71.

These were the rates for the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage from April 2019.

The National Living Wage started on 1 April 2024. It is for people aged 21 and over.

### Marriage Allowance

Marriage Allowance lets you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the money you can earn before you pay tax.

This reduces their tax by up to £252 in the tax year. The tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April the next year.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

To get a benefit as a couple, you must earn less than your Personal Allowance. You are the lower earner. Your Personal Allowance is usually £12,570.

You can calculate how much tax you could save as a couple. You should call the Income Tax helpline if you get other income. This income could be dividends, savings or benefits from your job. Call the helpline if you do not know your taxable income.

When you transfer some of your Personal Allowance, you might pay more tax yourself. But you could still pay less as a couple.

### Example

Your income is £11,500 and your Personal Allowance is £12,570. You do not pay tax.

Your partner's income is £20,000 and their Personal Allowance is £12,570. They pay tax on £7,430. This £7,430 is their 'taxable income'. As a couple, you are paying Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance, you transfer £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310. Your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

This means you will now pay tax on £190. Your partner will only pay tax on £6,170. As a couple, you benefit. You are only paying Income Tax on £6,360 instead of £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

### Who can apply

You can get Marriage Allowance if all these things are true:

- You are married or in a civil partnership.
- You do not pay Income Tax. Your income is below £12,570.
- Your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate. Their income is between £12,571 and £50,270 before they get Marriage Allowance.

You cannot claim Marriage Allowance if you live together but are not married or in a civil partnership.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic, or intermediate rate. Their income is usually between £12,571 and £43,662.

Your application for Marriage Allowance will not change if you or your partner:

- Are getting a pension.
- Live abroad. You must get a Personal Allowance.

If you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935, you might get more money. You could apply for Married Couple’s Allowance instead.

You cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple’s Allowance at the same time.

## Backdating your claim

Your partner's tax bill will be reduced.

## Stopping Marriage Allowance

This keeps going until you cancel Marriage Allowance.
You might cancel if your income changes.
You might cancel if your relationship ends.

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

To work out your rate:

- Work out your taxable income. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any other Income Tax reliefs.
- Work out your total taxable gains.
- Deduct your tax-free allowance from your total taxable gains.
- Add this amount to your taxable income.
- If this amount is within the basic Income Tax band, you pay 18% on gains from 6 April 2026.
- For any amount above the basic Income Tax band, you pay 24% on gains from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, deduct the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000, which leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The combined amount of £29,600 is less than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year). So, you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

You will pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, deduct the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000, which leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. The combined amount of £69,600 is more than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year). You will pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700. You will then pay 24% on £31,900.

You will pay £10,842.

### Inheritance Tax basics

Inheritance Tax is a tax on the estate of someone who has died.

The estate includes their property, money and possessions.

There is normally no Inheritance Tax to pay if either:

- the value of your estate is below the £325,000 threshold
- you leave everything above the £325,000 threshold to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club

You may still need to report the estate’s value even if it is below the threshold.

If you give away your home to your children or grandchildren your threshold can increase to £500,000.

Your children include adopted, foster or stepchildren.

If you are married or in a civil partnership your estate is worth less than your threshold.

Any unused threshold can be added to your partner’s threshold when you die.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Inheritance Tax rates

The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%.
It is only charged on the part of your estate that is above the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000.
Your tax-free threshold is £325,000.
The Inheritance Tax charged will be 40% of £175,000 (£500,000 minus £325,000).

The estate can pay Inheritance Tax at a reduced rate of 36% on some assets.
This happens if you leave 10% or more of the 'net value' to charity in your will.
The net value is the estate's total value minus any debts.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you give while you are alive may be taxed after your death.
Depending on when you gave the gift, 'taper relief' might mean the Inheritance Tax charged on the gift is less than 40%.

Other reliefs, such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, allow some assets to be passed on free of Inheritance Tax.
Other reliefs, such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, also allow some assets to be passed on with a reduced bill.

## Who pays the tax to HMRC

Money from your estate pays Inheritance Tax to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC).
The executor pays if there is a will.
The executor is the person who deals with the estate.

Your beneficiaries usually do not pay tax on what they inherit.
They might have other taxes to pay.
This can happen if they get rental income from a house left to them in a will.

People you give gifts to might have to pay Inheritance Tax.
They only pay if you give away more than £325,000.
They also only pay if you die within 7 years.

### What you pay

Your Medicare costs depend on your coverage. They also depend on the services you use. You can find costs for each part of Medicare. You can also learn what you pay out-of-pocket.

### What is a premium?

A premium is what you pay each month for Part A or Part B. You must pay this even if you do not use any medical care.

### What is a deductible?

A deductible is the amount you pay for covered services each year. You must pay this amount before your insurance pays.

### What is coinsurance?

Coinsurance is the part of the bill you pay for a service. Your insurance pays the rest. You pay a set percentage of the total cost.

### What is a copayment?

A copayment is a set dollar amount you pay for a service. Your insurance pays the rest of the bill. You pay this each time you get care.

### Late enrollment penalties

Sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period unless you have other similar coverage, like from an employer. If you do not sign up on time, you may have to pay an extra amount called a late enrollment penalty.

Late enrollment penalties:

- Are added to your monthly premium.
- Are not a one-time late fee.
- Are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage. For most people, this is a lifetime penalty. The Part A penalty is different.
- Go up the longer you wait to sign up. They are based on how long you go without coverage similar to Medicare. Find out when you should sign up to avoid penalties.

## Part A late enrollment penalty

- Some people must buy Part A.
- These people do not qualify for premium-free Part A.
- Do I qualify for premium-free Part A?
- If you must buy Part A, your monthly premium may go up 10%.
- You must wait to buy Part A if you do not buy it when you are first eligible for Medicare.
- You will have to pay the penalty.
- The penalty lasts for twice the number of years you did not sign up.

Example:
- If you were eligible for Part A for 2 years, you did not sign up.
- You will pay the higher premium for 4 years.
- Usually, you do not have to pay a penalty.
- This happens if you meet certain conditions.
- These conditions allow you to sign up for Part A during a Special Enrollment Period.
- Find out if you’re eligible for a Special Enrollment Period.

### Part B late enrollment penalty

- You usually do not pay a Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.
- You also do not pay a penalty if you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program.
- Learn more about Special Enrollment Periods.
- You pay an extra 10% for each year you could have signed up for Part B.
- You must pay this extra amount only if you did not sign up during that year.
- You may pay a higher premium if you earn more money.

Example:

- If you waited 2 full years (24 months) to sign up for Part B, you pay a 20% late enrollment penalty.
- You paid this because you did not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.
- The penalty is 10% for each full 12-month period that you could have signed up.
- You also pay the standard Part B monthly premium ($202.90 in 2026).

2026 Calculation:

- $202.90 (2026 Part B standard premium)
- + $40.58 (20% [of $202.90] late enrollment penalty)
- = $243.48

- $243.50 will be your Part B monthly premium for 2026.
- This amount ($243.48) is rounded to the nearest $.10.
- This total includes the late enrollment penalty.

### Part D late enrollment penalty

- You usually will not pay a Part D penalty if you have creditable drug coverage.
- Creditable drug coverage means coverage that is similar in value to Part D.
- You also will not pay a penalty if you qualify for Extra Help.
- You will pay an extra 1% for each month you do not join.
- That extra amount is 12% a year.
- You pay this extra if you do not join a Medicare drug plan when you first get Medicare.
- You pay this extra if you go 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage.
- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.
- After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty.
- The plan will also tell you what your premium will be.

### What if I don't agree with the Part D late enrollment penalty?

- If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan, you will pay a penalty.
- You must pay this penalty if you did not have creditable drug coverage.
- Your penalty will be 14% of the national base beneficiary premium.
- You will pay this 14% penalty in addition to your monthly plan premium.

- The penalty amount comes from the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026).
- The national base beneficiary premium changes each year.
- Your penalty amount may also change each year.
- This monthly penalty is added for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.
- You still pay this penalty even if you switch plans.

### In 2026:

- $38.99 (2026 national base beneficiary premium)
- X 0.14 (14% penalty)
- = $5.46 (rounded to the nearest $0.10 = $5.50)
- $5.50 will be your monthly penalty for 2026.
- This amount is added to your plan's monthly premium for 2026.

### If you (or your spouse) are still working when you turn 65, Medicare works a little differently

Medicare rules change a bit if you or your spouse are still working at age 65. Do you need a refresher on how Medicare works?

## Do I need to sign up for Medicare when I turn 65?

You can answer a few questions to find out when you should sign up. Or you can read the scenarios below.

### If you (or your spouse) have health insurance from a job:

If you or your spouse are still working, you may wait to sign up for Medicare. You might not have to pay a late penalty. This is true if you have group health insurance at your company. This insurance must be available to everyone at the company.

- If you do not pay a premium for Part A (Hospital Insurance), you can sign up when you turn 65. You can also sign up later. Do I qualify?
- You can wait until you (or your spouse) stop working. You can also wait until you lose your health insurance if that happens first. You do not have to pay a late penalty when you sign up for Part B (Medical Insurance).
- You have an 8-month Special Enrollment Period (SEP). You can sign up for Medicare in this time. You can also add Part B to your existing Part A coverage. The SEP starts when you stop working. It also starts if you lose your insurance. This is true even if you choose COBRA or other non-Medicare coverage.

Ask the employer that gives you health insurance. Ask if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. If you do not sign up for Part A and Part B, your job insurance might not cover your costs.

If you are self-employed, your rules may be different. This also applies if you have health insurance that is not available to everyone at your company, like retiree coverage.

Ask your insurance provider if your coverage is an employer group health plan. The IRS defines this plan type. If it is not this type of plan, sign up for Medicare when you turn 65. Do not sign up late or you will pay a monthly Part B penalty.

If you have retiree coverage from a past job, it may not pay for your health services. This is true if you do not have both Medicare Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance). Ask your benefits administrator how your retiree coverage works with Medicare.

Do not risk losing your retiree coverage. Check before joining a plan.
The employer might offer coverage if you have Medicare. Examples include a supplemental plan, drug coverage, or a Medicare Advantage Plan. If they offer these, ask if you or your family will lose retiree coverage if you join a plan the employer does not offer. Get more information about retiree coverage & Medicare.

### If you have health insurance that's not from a job:

This includes insurance from Medicaid, the Marketplace, or another private company.

Answer a few questions to find out when to sign up for Medicare. This gives you other important information based on your specific coverage type.

The rules change depending on what other health insurance you have. Contact your health insurance plan to get more information.

This also includes insurance you bought with a stipend from work.

Ask your health insurance company if you need to sign up for Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you turn 65. Some private insurance companies have rules that lower what they pay. They might not pay at all if you are eligible for other coverage like Medicare. Once you sign up, Medicare pays first.

### If you have COBRA coverage:

If your job offered you COBRA coverage after your employment ended, the rules may vary. This is true if you lost coverage as the dependent of the covered employee. This applies if you have not signed up for Medicare yet.

- Sign up for Medicare when you turn 65. This avoids gaps in coverage. It also avoids a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty.
- Your COBRA coverage will probably end once you sign up.

Do not wait until your COBRA coverage ends to sign up for Part B. COBRA coverage does not extend your limited time to sign up for Medicare.

Get important information about COBRA and Medicare.

And you got COBRA after you signed up for Medicare.

COBRA pays after Medicare. This is true unless you have End-Stage Renal Disease.

Get important information about COBRA and Medicare.

### If you don't have health insurance: And you're still working.

- Sign up for both Part A (Hospital Insurance) and Part B (Medical Insurance) when you are first eligible. This is usually when you turn 65. If you sign up later, you may have to pay a penalty.
- If you cannot afford insurance, there are ways to get help paying costs.

## Your first chance to sign up (Initial Enrollment Period)

You usually sign up when you turn 65. This time is called your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before you turn 65. It ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.

My birthday is on the first of the month.

Avoid the penalty
If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up. You may also have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty. You pay this penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage. The penalty goes up the longer you wait. You may also have to pay a penalty if you have to pay a Part A premium. This is also called "Premium-Part A." Learn more about how to avoid late enrollment penalties.

### When your coverage starts

The date your coverage starts depends on which month you sign up during your Initial Enrollment Period. Your coverage always starts on the first of the month.

If you qualify for premium-free Part A: Your Part A coverage starts the month you turn 65. (If your birthday is on the first of the month, coverage starts the month before you turn 65.)

Part B (and premium-Part A): Coverage starts based on the month you sign up:

| If you sign up: | Coverage starts: |
| Before the month you turn 65 | The month you turn 65 |
| The month you turn 65, or during the 3 months after | The next month |

### Signing up for premium-free Part A later

You can sign up for Part A any time after you turn 65. Your Part A coverage starts 6 months back from when you sign up. It also starts 6 months back from when you apply for benefits from Social Security (or the Railroad Retirement Board). Coverage can't start earlier than the month you turned 65.

## Between January 1-March 31 each year (General Enrollment Period)

You can sign up between January 1-March 31 each year. This time is called the General Enrollment Period. Your coverage starts the month after you sign up. You might pay a monthly late enrollment penalty if you do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. Get details about the late enrollment penalties.

### Costs for Medicare drug coverage
Your total costs for Medicare drug coverage will depend on which plan you choose. Depending on the plan, you could pay:

- **Premium**: You pay this monthly amount for coverage. You pay this amount even if you do not get covered drugs.
- Your specific premium depends on the plan you choose. You may have to pay more if your income is higher. Who pays a higher Part D premium because of income?
- If you have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty, it is added to your monthly premium.

**Tip**: You should consider a drug plan with a low monthly premium. This helps you avoid the late enrollment penalty. You can do this even if you do not take many drugs now. You can also do this if your current out-of-pocket drug costs are low. All plans must cover a wide range of drugs that people with Medicare take.

- **Deductible**: You pay this amount for covered drugs and items each year. You pay this before your plan starts to pay. Your deductible depends on which plan you choose. No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $700 in 2027 ($615 in 2026). Some plans have no deductible.
- **Copayment**: You pay this fixed amount for a drug at the pharmacy.
- **Coinsurance**: You pay this percentage for a drug at the pharmacy.

## Medicare drug coverage stages

Most Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage Plans with drug coverage have 3 stages:

- Deductible stage: If your plan has a deductible, you pay all costs yourself. You keep paying until you reach the full deductible. No plan may have a deductible over $615 in 2026 ($700 in 2027). Some plans do not have a deductible.
- Initial coverage stage: After you reach your full deductible, pay 25% of the cost as coinsurance. This applies to your generic and brand-name drugs. You pay this until your out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027). This total includes payments made for you, like through the Extra Help program. Then, you automatically get "catastrophic coverage."
- Catastrophic coverage stage: You will not pay out-of-pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

When you have Medicare drug coverage, you get an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) the month after the pharmacy bills your plan. Your EOB shows the prescriptions you filled. It shows what your plan paid. It shows what you and others paid. It shows your coverage stage. It shows what counts toward your out-of-pocket costs. It shows what counts toward your total drug costs.

## How do I pay my plan’s premium?

You can choose to pay your premium in these ways:

- Your plan takes the money from your checking or savings account.
- You use a credit or debit card (fees may apply).
- Your plan sends you a bill each month. Some plans bill in advance for next month’s coverage. Send your payment to the plan—not to Medicare. Contact your plan for their payment address.
- Your plan takes the money from your Social Security payment. Contact your plan—not Social Security—to ask for this payment option. It may take up to 3 months to start. In cases where premiums weren’t withheld from your Social Security payment until 1 or 2 months after you joined a Medicare drug plan, you’ll get a bill for the months your drug plan’s premiums weren’t withheld. You’ll need to pay your drug plan’s monthly premium directly to your plan for those months. Your plan will tell you when your premium withholding from your Social Security payment is set up.

## How can I lower my drug costs?

If you qualify, programs can lower your drug costs.

- Medicaid is a joint federal and state program. It helps cover medical costs for some people with limited income and resources. Each state has different income and resource requirements. These requirements determine who is eligible. Contact your state to find out if you are eligible.
- Extra Help is a Medicare program. It helps pay your drug costs. You automatically qualify for Extra Help if you qualify for Medicaid. You also qualify automatically if you qualify for one of the Medicare Savings Programs. You also qualify if you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits from Social Security. If you do not automatically qualify for Extra Help, you can apply.

- Medicare's Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET) is a Medicare program. It gives temporary Medicare Part D drug coverage. This coverage is for people who qualify for Extra Help or Medicaid. It is for people who are not enrolled in a Medicare drug plan yet. LI NET covers all Part D covered drugs. There are no network pharmacy restrictions.

- State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (SPAP) are state programs. These programs provide coverage from your state. They also provide coverage from the U.S. Virgin Islands. They help pay your drug plan premiums. They also help pay cost sharing. SPAP contributions may count toward your Medicare drug coverage out-of-pocket limit. Eligibility depends on each program's specific rules.

- Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (sometimes called Patient Assistance Programs (PAPs)) are programs from some pharmaceutical companies. They help pay for medications. They help people enrolled in Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Find out if there is a Pharmaceutical Assistance Program (PAP). Find a program that can lower prescription costs for the drugs you take. Each company has different eligibility requirements. Contact the company to find out if you are eligible. Start getting help.

The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is a new payment option. It works with your current Medicare drug coverage. It helps you manage your out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by your plan. It spreads these costs across the calendar year. The calendar year is January–December. This payment option might help you manage your monthly expenses. It does not save you money. It does not lower your drug costs.

## What's the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The Part D late enrollment penalty is an amount added to your monthly Part D premium.
This amount is added forever.
You may owe this penalty if you go without Part D or other creditable prescription drug coverage for 63 or more days in a row after your Initial Enrollment Period ends.
After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you must pay a penalty.
The plan will also tell you what your premium will be.
You will usually pay the penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

### How much is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The penalty is 1% times the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026) times the number of full, uncovered months.
These are the months you were eligible for Medicare drug coverage but did not join (and did not have other creditable prescription drug coverage).
The result is rounded to the nearest $.10.
This rounded amount is added to your monthly premium.
The "national base beneficiary premium" may go up each year.
Your penalty amount may also go up each year because of this.

Example: If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan without creditable drug coverage, you must pay a 14% late enrollment penalty.
You pay this penalty in addition to your monthly plan premium.

### Appeal when a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient with observation services"

A court order gives you the right to appeal. The hospital can change your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient." This rule applies if you meet certain criteria.

You can ask for an appeal if you were admitted as an inpatient on or after January 1, 2009. Your status changed to "outpatient getting observation services." You must also meet certain other criteria. Learn how to file this type of appeal.

You can ask for a fast appeal while you are still in the hospital. The hospital must have changed your status from inpatient to "outpatient getting observation services." Learn how to file this type of appeal.

### Why does hospital status matter?

Your hospital status affects how much you pay for hospital services. Your hospital status may also affect if Medicare covers care. This care happens in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after your hospital stay.
